title: A manufactured uterus that supports pregnancy without a donor graft and chronic immunosuppression

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a complete manufactured uterus that enables a recipient to carry a pregnancy without depending on a donated uterine organ or chronic systemic immunosuppression. It would need to support embryo implantation, formation and function of the placenta, adaptation of the uterine blood supply, growth throughout pregnancy, and safe delivery. The target is an organ that performs these functions together, rather than a tissue patch that repairs part of an existing uterus.

Concept definition: growing the organ from the recipient’s own cells is one possible route, but the innovation does not require every cell to be autologous. Another design could qualify if it supplies a complete functional uterus, avoids chronic systemic immunosuppression, and is independent of donated uterine organs and scaffolds. Donor independence and immune acceptance are separate requirements: removing cells from a donated uterus and repopulating its scaffold might address some immune problems while retaining a dependence on donated uterine material.

significance.text: Donor uterus transplantation has established a path to childbearing for some people with absolute uterine-factor infertility. The supplied U.S. cohort documents pregnancies and births within a care pathway involving living or deceased donors, postoperative immunosuppression, and recipient graft hysterectomy. A manufactured uterus meeting the proposed requirements would extend gestational capacity to a supplied organ while removing two specific dependencies: a donated uterus and chronic systemic immunosuppression. That would constitute a substantial new reproductive capability.

Conditional implications: reproducible manufacture could eventually make treatment less dependent on donor availability and could avoid risks specifically associated with prolonged systemic immunosuppression. Wider access, larger treatment volumes, and lower overall risk remain possibilities rather than established consequences. They would depend on manufacturing reliability, implantation procedures, pregnancy outcomes, costs, clinical capacity, and access. Successful pregnancies in a few recipients would not establish that the overall treatment is safer or more scalable than transplantation.

The analogy to replacing a donated organ has an important limit: supplying viable uterine tissue is only part of the goal. Rabbit reconstruction and primate scaffold experiments provide relevant engineering foundations, but the reproductive endpoint requires coordinated function over an entire pregnancy. Likewise, keeping a donated uterus alive outside the body could advance organ research or preservation without demonstrating either donor independence or gestation in a manufactured organ.

missing_breakthrough.text: The capability to establish is a complete human-scale organ that integrates implantation, placentation, vascular adaptation, structural growth, and safe delivery without donated uterine material or chronic systemic immunosuppression. The supplied studies demonstrate components of this problem, including reconstruction of uterine segments and production and recellularization of uterine scaffolds. They do not demonstrate the complete target capability. Because the supplied review contains no bounded freshness search, this evidence gap cannot establish that no other demonstration existed anywhere in the field as of November 1, 2026.

Engineering synthesis: a useful organ would need a blood supply that connects reliably to the recipient and adapts as pregnancy develops, together with uterine tissue that supports implantation and placental interaction. Preserving a scaffold’s architecture or showing that cells can repopulate it does not establish that the reconstructed organ can sustain these changing demands. Vascular anatomy and function therefore remain central integration challenges, rather than problems resolved by the presence of a scaffold alone.

Immune compatibility must be demonstrated at the level of the functioning organ and pregnancy. Autologous cell-seeded rabbit constructs provide evidence for one regenerative approach, while the baboon scaffold study includes recellularization and immune-response assays. Neither result establishes immune acceptance of a complete manufactured human uterus during pregnancy. In particular, in vitro assays using rat mesenchymal stem cells cannot establish that a human recipient would avoid chronic systemic immunosuppression.

Engineering synthesis: the organ must also retain structural integrity as it enlarges and stretches during pregnancy, and permit a defined safe delivery pathway. Labor need not be mandatory if safe delivery can be achieved another way. The primate study’s motivation includes defective uterine tissue and uterine rupture, underscoring that tissue viability alone is an insufficient functional endpoint. These vascular, immune, and mechanical challenges are a useful account of the integration problem, not an exhaustive experimentally established list of all barriers.

current_state.text: O’Neill and colleagues reported 60 U.S. uterus transplants performed from February 2016 through December 2025 in an article published online September 29, 2026. By December 2025, 42 of 60 recipients, or 70.0%, had achieved at least one live birth or ongoing clinical pregnancy, and 48 neonates had been born. The 70.0% figure combines births and ongoing pregnancies; it is not a live-birth rate. Median gestational age at delivery was 36 5/7 weeks, and 58.3% of neonates were born preterm. These are outcomes of donor transplantation, not manufactured-organ pregnancies.

The cohort abstract describes living and deceased donors, postoperative immunosuppression and monitoring, fertility and obstetric care, recipient graft hysterectomy, and neonatal and pediatric follow-up. This documents the relevant donor and immune-treatment dependencies within that clinical pathway. The supplied abstract does not establish a universal requirement for cesarean delivery or a mandatory graft-removal schedule for every recipient, and those broader claims should not be inferred from it.

In 2020, Magalhaes and colleagues reported uterine reconstruction in rabbits after subtotal uterine excision using constructs seeded with autologous cells. Four of ten rabbits receiving cell-seeded constructs had normal pregnancies in the reconstructed uterine segment, supporting fetal development to term and live birth; normal pregnancies in the reconstructed segment were reported only in that group. This is evidence of functional segment reconstruction. Native proximal and distal tissue remained, but the inspected abstract and figure captions do not establish how much of the original uterus was retained. Describing it as still mostly present would therefore overstate the available detail. The review did not inspect the figure images or full paper.

De Miguel-Gómez and colleagues reported decellularization of baboon uteri, in vitro recellularization of the resulting scaffolds with xenogeneic rat bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells, and immune-response assays. The study was published online December 6, 2024, and appeared in the March 2025 issue of Acta Obstetricia et Gynecologica Scandinavica, volume 104, pages 483–493. The abstract examined in the supplied review reports no pregnancy demonstration. These findings concern scaffold preparation and laboratory characterization; they do not establish whole-organ pregnancy function or immune acceptance during human gestation. The complete paper was not part of the reviewed evidence.

A March 28, 2026 MIT Technology Review article by Jessica Hamzelou described a Carlos Simon Foundation experiment in which a donated human uterus was reportedly maintained by perfusion outside the body for one day. The article stated that the work was unpublished at that time and described plans to use embryo-like structures rather than human embryos. This is a news account of short-term donated-organ maintenance, not independent validation of a manufactured uterus or a pregnancy demonstration. The proposed experiments with embryo-like structures were plans, not reported gestational achievements.

The earlier research attributed an estimate of Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome prevalence of about one in 4,500 female births, and graft removal within several years to limit immunosuppression, to a 2022 Reproductive BioMedicine Online review. No retained text from that review was supplied, so those specific assertions remain unverified within this record. This access limitation does not negate the independently documented transplant outcomes or use of immunosuppression.

Taken together, the dated evidence establishes clinical childbearing through donor transplantation, pregnancy-capable uterine segment reconstruction in rabbits, laboratory work on primate uterine scaffolds, and a reported short-term human organ-perfusion experiment. None of these supplied reports demonstrates a complete donor-independent manufactured human uterus carrying a pregnancy without chronic systemic immunosuppression. The review’s clinical and engineering evidence is principally abstract-level, with rabbit figure captions also available and the news article available in full. No bounded freshness search was supplied, so this account describes the documented results rather than a comprehensive determination of the field’s status on November 1, 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed initial demonstration: a complete manufactured uterus, independent of donated uterine organs or scaffolds, supports an uncomplicated human pregnancy and a healthy live birth without chronic systemic immunosuppression, with successful pregnancy and birth repeated in at least one additional recipient. This is a proposed threshold for initial functional feasibility, not an established clinical or regulatory standard.
completion_criteria.label: Repeated uncomplicated pregnancies and healthy births without chronic systemic immunosuppression

completion_criteria.text: Proposed outcome definitions: protocols should prospectively define uncomplicated pregnancy, healthy birth, follow-up duration, and any permitted temporary immunosuppression. They should document implantation and placental function, uterine blood supply and structural integrity, the delivery pathway, and recipient and child outcomes over the defined follow-up period. Any temporary immune treatment should be reported explicitly so that the claim of freedom from chronic systemic immunosuppression can be assessed.
completion_criteria.label: Prospectively defined outcomes with documented follow-up and temporary immunosuppression

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility criteria: successful outcomes should involve independently manufactured organs in different recipients, with the manufacturing methods, scaffold origins, cell sources, implantation procedures, and failures reported sufficiently to evaluate repeatability. A donated uterus, a donor-derived uterine scaffold, an animal repair patch, or brief perfusion outside the body would not satisfy the complete target. The proposal does not impose a requirement that the organ cost as little as ordinary surgical mesh; it does require genuine independence from donated uterine material.
completion_criteria.label: Independent organ manufacturing reproduced across recipients with donor independence documented

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: repeated births would establish demonstrated function in the recipients and conditions studied. They would not establish suitability for every cause of uterine-factor infertility, every recipient, or every pregnancy, nor would they establish population-level safety, affordability, or scalable supply. Those broader claims would require further clinical follow-up, manufacturing evidence, and comparative assessment.
completion_criteria.label: Demonstrated function limited to the recipients and conditions studied

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: OBG-03, Extrauterine physiological support across the viability gap, concerns support outside the uterus. OBG-08 instead supplies a uterus that itself supports implantation and gestation. Both address reproductive support, but an artificial placenta or extrauterine support system does not meet the manufactured-organ requirement.

Roster-based synthesis: OBG-01, Causal control of the human parturition clock, overlaps with the timing and management of delivery, but controlling labor does not supply a missing uterus. OBG-04, In utero reversal of placental insufficiency, concerns restoration of placental function within a pregnancy; OBG-08 must support placentation but does not by itself establish treatment of placental insufficiency. OBG-10, Restoration of the amniotic compartment after preterm membrane rupture, addresses another pregnancy-support function that successful uterine manufacture would not automatically solve.

Roster-based synthesis: OBG-02, Manufacture of a functional human oocyte from a somatic cell, and OBG-05, Reversal of human ovarian reproductive aging, address reproductive limitations involving oocytes and ovarian function. They could be complementary to uterine manufacture for someone with multiple causes of infertility, but neither supplies gestational capacity, and a manufactured uterus does not establish functional oocyte production or ovarian rejuvenation.

Roster-based synthesis: OBG-06, In utero molecular correction of fetal-onset genetic disease, concerns treatment of the fetus during an established pregnancy rather than manufacture of the gestational organ. OBG-07, A mechanism-based cure for endometriosis, and OBG-09, Fertility-preserving interception of high-grade serous tubo-ovarian carcinoma, concern disease treatment or interception while preserving reproductive function. Their overlap with OBG-08 is the broader aim of enabling reproduction; replacing uterine capacity does not constitute a cure for endometriosis, cancer interception, or fetal genetic correction. These remain distinct entries.

change_log.change: Preserved OBG-08’s identity while defining donor independence and freedom from chronic systemic immunosuppression as separate requirements.
change_log.reason: A donor-derived decellularized scaffold could address some immune concerns while preserving dependence on donated uterine material.

change_log.change: Integrated implantation, placentation, vascular adaptation, pregnancy-associated growth, structural integrity, and safe delivery into the functional target and engineering discussion.
change_log.reason: The innovation requires coordinated whole-organ pregnancy function; viable tissue or scaffold preparation alone is insufficient.

change_log.change: Retained autologous cells as a possible implementation rather than a mandatory design constraint.
change_log.reason: The concept is defined by function, immune requirements, and donor independence rather than one cell-source strategy.

change_log.change: Replaced guaranteed improvements in scale and overall risk with conditional benefits requiring additional evidence.
change_log.reason: Initial successful pregnancies would remove specific dependencies but would not establish comparative safety, affordability, manufacturing capacity, or access.

change_log.change: Preserved the U.S. cohort’s 60 transplants, 42 recipients reaching the combined endpoint, and 48 neonates, and added the exact delivery median and preterm proportion.
change_log.reason: The reviewed abstract supports these figures; the 70.0% endpoint combines live birth and ongoing clinical pregnancy and must not be described as a live-birth rate.

change_log.change: Confined immunosuppression and graft hysterectomy statements to the documented transplant care pathway and removed universal cesarean and graft-removal requirements.
change_log.reason: The supplied abstract does not establish those requirements for every recipient.

change_log.change: Replaced the assertion that the rabbit uterus was still mostly present with the supported description of subtotal excision and retained native tissue.
change_log.reason: The abstract and figure captions establish segment reconstruction but do not quantify the proportion of uterus retained.

change_log.change: Specified the baboon scaffold study’s online and issue dates, rat cell source, laboratory scope, and absence of a pregnancy outcome in the inspected abstract.
change_log.reason: These distinctions prevent scaffold recellularization and immune assays from being interpreted as demonstrated whole-organ pregnancy function or human immune acceptance.

change_log.change: Preserved the one-day human perfusion report with its donated-organ origin, unpublished status at reporting, and planned embryo-like-structure experiments.
change_log.reason: The news account supports these attributed details but does not independently validate gestation or manufactured-organ function.

change_log.change: Retained the 2022 review’s prevalence and graft-removal assertions only as explicitly unverified attributions.
change_log.reason: No retained source text was supplied; missing evidence warrants qualification rather than treating the assertions as verified or false.

change_log.change: Made the completion threshold explicitly proposed, defined repetition across recipients, and added outcome, follow-up, and temporary-immunosuppression requirements.
change_log.reason: A convincing initial demonstration needs assessable boundaries and must not be mistaken for an established standard or proof of universal applicability.

change_log.change: Qualified the present-day absence claim and preserved the review’s partial-document and freshness limitations.
change_log.reason: The supplied dated results do not demonstrate the target, but no bounded freshness search establishes the entire field’s status on November 1, 2026.

change_log.change: Explained relationships with every other supplied roster entry without merging their identities.
change_log.reason: Shared reproductive goals do not make organ manufacture equivalent to oocyte production, pregnancy support, disease treatment, or fertility preservation.

unresolved_issues: The supplied materials do not establish whether a complete donor-independent manufactured uterus had supported a human pregnancy anywhere in the field by November 1, 2026; no bounded freshness search was supplied.
The 2022 review’s estimate of approximately one MRKH case per 4,500 female births and its specific graft-removal timing remain unverified because no retained text was available.
The reviewed rabbit material does not quantify the proportion of native uterine tissue retained after subtotal excision.
The primate study’s full paper was not included in the reviewed evidence; the absence of a reported pregnancy demonstration is bounded to the inspected abstract.
Independent validation and subsequent publication of the one-day human uterus perfusion experiment are not established by the supplied March 2026 news account.
The proposed demonstration still requires prospective operational definitions of uncomplicated pregnancy, healthy birth, follow-up duration, and acceptable temporary immunosuppression.
Comparative overall safety, manufacturing reproducibility at scale, affordability, and access remain unestablished even if initial pregnancy and birth criteria are eventually met.

brief.title: A manufactured uterus for carrying a pregnancy
possible: People who cannot carry a pregnancy because they lack a functioning uterus could receive a manufactured replacement. This organ, where a pregnancy grows, would support pregnancy through safe delivery without donated uterine material or long-term drugs that suppress the body’s immune defenses.
why: Treatment could become less dependent on finding an organ donor. Recipients could also avoid the risks specifically associated with prolonged immune suppression.

sources.showed: Their U.S. study reported 48 babies born after donated uterus transplants. Treatment included drugs to suppress immune defenses.
sources.quote: No life-threatening complications or mortality occurred.
sources.cited_for: Donated uterus transplants already provide a path to childbearing.
sources.not_established: These births do not demonstrate pregnancy in a manufactured uterus.

sources.who: Authors of the Reproductive BioMedicine Online review
sources.showed: This is a review discussing a condition involving an absent uterus and removal of transplanted uteruses to limit immune suppression.
sources.cited_for: It provides background on uterus transplantation and immune treatment.
sources.not_established: A review of transplantation does not demonstrate a functioning manufactured uterus.

sources.who: Renata S Magalhaes and colleagues at Wake Forest
sources.showed: They repaired rabbit uterine segments using manufactured supports carrying the animals’ own cells. Pregnancies in the repaired segments reached live birth.
sources.quote: had normal pregnancies (four in ten) in the reconstructed segment of the uterus and supported fetal development to term and live birth.
sources.cited_for: Engineered uterine tissue can support pregnancy within a repaired animal organ.
sources.not_established: Native uterine tissue remained; this was not a complete manufactured replacement.

sources.showed: They removed cells from baboon uteruses while preserving their supporting framework, called a scaffold. Rat cells could grow on these scaffolds in laboratory tests.
sources.quote: The chorioallantoic membrane assay and in vitro recellularization experiments confirmed that the scaffolds were bioactive and non-cytotoxic.
sources.cited_for: Uterine scaffolds can retain useful structure and support added cells.
sources.not_established: Laboratory tests do not establish pregnancy function, human immune acceptance or independence from donated uterine material.

sources.who: Javier González, Xavier Santamaria and the Carlos Simon Foundation team
sources.showed: In an unpublished experiment reported in a news article, the team kept a donated human uterus alive outside the body for a day by pumping blood through it.
sources.quote: “We kept it alive for one day,” says Santamaria.
sources.cited_for: A donated human uterus can reportedly be maintained briefly outside the body.
sources.not_established: The experiment did not demonstrate a manufactured organ or pregnancy, and independent confirmation remains unestablished.

shown: Magalhaes and colleagues reached live birth after repairing rabbit uterine segments with the animals’ own cells. This is the closest pregnancy result described for engineered tissue. It came from a small animal study with native uterine tissue still attached.
missing: A complete manufactured uterus still needs to support an embryo attaching, the placenta forming and the blood supply adapting throughout pregnancy.
The organ must remain intact as it stretches and grows, and allow safe delivery.
Immune acceptance throughout pregnancy must be demonstrated without long-term immune suppression.
Repeatable manufacture must work without donated uteruses or their supporting frameworks.

milestones.label: Repeated healthy births without long-term immune suppression
milestones.explanation: Complete manufactured uteruses without donated uterine material would have to support uncomplicated pregnancies and healthy births in different recipients. This would establish initial functional feasibility.

milestones.label: Defined outcomes, follow-up and temporary immune treatment
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to define success and follow-up beforehand, document organ function and delivery, and report temporary immune treatment. This would make pregnancy, recipient and child outcomes assessable.

milestones.label: Repeatable manufacture without donated uterine material
milestones.explanation: Separately manufactured organs would have to succeed across recipients, with material origins, methods and failures documented. This would establish repeatability and independence from donated uterine material.

milestones.label: Function established within the conditions studied
milestones.explanation: Results would have to establish which recipients and conditions supported successful pregnancies. This would define demonstrated use; broader safety, affordability and supply would require further evidence.

uncertain: What should count as an uncomplicated pregnancy and a healthy birth, and how long should recipients and children be followed?
How much temporary immune suppression would be compatible with the goal?
Would successful pregnancies translate into lower overall risk, affordable treatment and reliable supply at scale?

page.title: Bioengineered uterus
page.definition: A complete manufactured uterus supports embryo implantation, placental development and pregnancy to live birth in a human recipient. It uses neither a donated uterine organ nor a donor-derived uterine scaffold and requires no maintenance systemic immunosuppression, meaning ongoing drugs to prevent graft rejection.

goal.need: A U.S. cohort of 60 donor uterus transplants performed between February 2016 and December 2025 recorded 48 newborns. Care included postoperative immunosuppression, and complications required reoperation in recipients and living donors. Whole-organ manufacture targets the donor-organ and immunosuppression requirements of this route to pregnancy.

figures.caption: Complications requiring reoperation in the U.S. donor uterus transplantation cohort

statements.quote: the next step is to construct a complete uterus.
statements.context: Edina Sehic describes the research group's progression from engineered uterine segments to a replacement organ.

statements.body: Wake Forest Institute for Regenerative Medicine
statements.quote: avoids the risk of rejection and the need for antirejection drugs.
statements.context: The statement describes constructing uterine tissue using a patient's own cells.

completion.title: A manufactured uterus supports a human live birth without graft-directed systemic immunosuppression.
completion.criterion: One human recipient carries a pregnancy from implantation to delivery in a complete manufactured uterus made without a donated uterine organ or donor-derived uterine scaffold. No graft-directed systemic immunosuppression is given from uterine implantation through delivery. The newborn meets the 2025 International Glossary definition: delivery after 22 completed weeks of gestation with breathing or another sign of life after separation; birth weight of at least 500 g substitutes when gestational age is unknown.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback combining the developers' organ-replacement goal with published transplantation and fertility endpoints.
completion.basis: Searches of FDA and EMA pages, ClinicalTrials.gov, uterine-engineering reviews and developer statements found no whole-organ success test covering donor independence and immunosuppression. This fallback combines the developers’ replacement-organ goal with the field’s live-birth endpoint. Zero graft-directed systemic immunosuppression provides an unambiguous sufficient test without inventing a duration for chronic treatment.

milestones.title: An engineered uterine segment supports fetal development and live birth in a rabbit.
milestones.criterion: Fetal development occurs in the reconstructed uterine segment, and offspring are alive at delivery. The rabbit study published on 29 June 2020 assessed fetal location and newborn viability after subtotal reconstruction with autologous-cell constructs. Its reproductive group contained 14 rabbits; Table 1 records pregnancies in the engineered segment in 4/14. Native uterine tissue remained. This establishes segmental reproductive function.
milestones.set_by: Magalhaes and colleagues, published rabbit reproductive-study protocol; the endpoint concerns subtotal uterine reconstruction.
milestones.threshold_quote: Our reproductive studies showed that autologous tissue engineered constructs supported late-stage pregnancies and viable live births.

milestones.title: A complete manufactured uterus supports a live birth in a non-human mammal.
milestones.criterion: A complete manufactured uterine organ supports implantation, pregnancy and live offspring in an animal recipient, without a donated uterus, a donor-derived uterine scaffold or graft-directed systemic immunosuppression. A patch in a retained uterine body does not qualify. The rabbit segment births and the 2025 baboon scaffold bioactivity and recellularization assays do not demonstrate this whole-organ result.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; searches of developer publications and preclinical uterine-engineering literature found no published whole-organ animal gestation threshold.

milestones.title: A manufactured uterus survives 30 days and produces menstrual or withdrawal bleeding within 90 days.
milestones.criterion: In a human recipient, a complete manufactured uterine implant remains viable on postoperative day 30 and produces menstrual bleeding, or hormonally induced withdrawal bleeding, by day 90. These are the consortium's technical-survival and first-function endpoints. Its 2022 donor-transplant cohort met the day-30 endpoint in 25/33 recipients; that is evidence for the clinical benchmark, not for manufactured grafts.
milestones.set_by: United States Uterus Transplant Consortium, 2020 guidance, sections 3.1–3.2; written for donated grafts and applied here as graft-function benchmarks.
milestones.threshold_quote: 30-day graft survival in stage 1; menstruation by 90 days

milestones.title: A manufactured uterus supports a human pregnancy with ultrasound-confirmed fetal cardiac activity.
milestones.criterion: After embryo transfer, ultrasound identifies a gestational sac and a fetus with discernible cardiac activity inside a complete manufactured uterus. The 2025 glossary defines the cardiac-activity endpoint; the transplant consortium places clinical pregnancy before pregnancy maintenance and delivery.
milestones.set_by: ICMART and endorsing societies including ASRM and ESHRE, 2025 International Glossary, published in 2026; a general reproductive endpoint.
milestones.threshold_quote: A pregnancy diagnosed by ultrasonographic or clinical documentation of at least one fetus with discernible cardiac activity.

milestones.title: A complete manufactured uterus maintains a human pregnancy until delivery.
milestones.criterion: A pregnancy in a complete manufactured uterus continues until delivery with the fetus alive. This uses the consortium's pregnancy-maintenance stage, which precedes its live-born-delivery stage and specifies no separate gestational-week cutoff. Live birth remains the completion endpoint.
milestones.set_by: United States Uterus Transplant Consortium, 2020 guidance, section 3.1, stage 4; written for donated grafts and applied here as a gestational-function benchmark.

not_found: No registered human trial or published human pregnancy using a complete donor-independent manufactured uterus was found in searches through 14 November 2026.
No whole-organ animal pregnancy satisfying the donor-material and immunosuppression conditions was found.
The supplied PubMed page for the 2026 U.S. cohort did not render readable article text; its abstract was available in indexed search results.
The supplied 2022 Reproductive BioMedicine Online review could not be opened.
The supplied MIT Technology Review article dated 28 March 2026 could not be opened.
